accroche: The agricultural surplus was supposed to make the monument possible. At Göbekli Tepe, the monument comes first
contenu_vulgarise:
The standard story of prehistory comes down to an order of events. Nomadic hunter-gatherers settle down, domesticate plants and animals, build up surpluses, and those surpluses finally make possible what feeds no one: monuments, sanctuaries, specialists who do not produce.

Göbekli Tepe, in what is now southeastern Turkey, turns that order upside down.

## What is found there

The site is an artificial hill. Beneath the surface are enclosures organized around T-shaped pillars cut from limestone, several meters tall and weighing several tons.

These pillars are carved in bas-relief: foxes, wild boars, snakes, scorpions, birds. Some have folded arms and hands, which makes them stylized figures rather than mere supports.

Quarrying, cutting, moving, and raising such blocks requires a large, coordinated workforce, fed for the whole duration of the project.

## The dating problem

The first monumental constructions are dated to around 9600 BCE.

At that date, in that region, agriculture does not exist. No domesticated cereals, no herds, no pottery, no metal. The faunal remains at the site are those of wild animals (gazelles, aurochs), and the tools are chipped stone.

So it was hunter-gatherers who built this. The expected order no longer holds: the monumental comes before the agricultural surplus instead of flowing from it.

## The reverse hypothesis, and what it is worth

Klaus Schmidt, who directed the excavations starting in 1995, proposed reversing the causality. It would not be agriculture that made the sanctuary possible. It would be the building project that made agriculture necessary: regularly feeding teams brought together to build would have pushed people to intensify the harvesting of wild cereals, then to cultivate them.

The hypothesis is appealing, and it is debated. Recent campaigns have also changed the picture. Domestic-type buildings, hearths, burials beneath floors, and water-collection systems have been uncovered on the site, which seriously weakens the image of an isolated sanctuary visited only by pilgrims from afar.

What withstands these revisions is the negative fact. Whatever the exact use of the place, sanctuary or village, societies without agriculture were able to mobilize enough collective labor to raise multi-ton monoliths.

The surplus was therefore not the condition of the monument. It was perhaps its consequence, and at the very least, the order of causes that we took to be obvious was only a habit of storytelling.

repere.texte: The first monumental enclosures at Göbekli Tepe are dated to around 9600 BCE, several centuries before the first domesticated cereals in the region.
repere.source: Schmidt, “Göbekli Tepe – the Stone Age Sanctuaries,” Documenta Praehistorica, 37, 2010

carte.idee: Göbekli Tepe was built around 9600 BCE by societies with no agriculture, no herds, and no pottery. The agricultural surplus was therefore not the condition of the monument. Perhaps it was its consequence.

quiz.question: Why does the dating of Göbekli Tepe pose a problem for the standard account?
choix: Because the site is more recent than the earliest known Mesopotamian cities
Because the sculptures there are more elaborate than those of later periods
Because societies without agriculture mobilized considerable collective labor there
Because the tools found on site are made of metal, a material unknown at that time
quiz.explication: The usual account makes agricultural surplus the condition of the monumental. Yet the oldest layers of the site yield no domesticated cereals, no herds, no pottery, no metal; only chipped stone and wild fauna. It is the order of causes that is at issue, not the relative chronology of the site or the quality of its reliefs.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the bas-reliefs carved on the T-shaped pillars of Göbekli Tepe depict?
choix: Agricultural scenes showing the harvest of wild cereals
Wild animals: foxes, wild boars, snakes, scorpions, birds
Abstract geometric patterns, with no animal figuration at all
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The pillars bear bas-reliefs of foxes, wild boars, snakes, scorpions, and birds. Some of the pillars themselves have folded arms and hands, which makes them stylized figures rather than mere supports.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What hypothesis does Klaus Schmidt propose to explain the link between the building project and agriculture?
choix: That the need to feed the construction teams pushed people to cultivate wild cereals
That agriculture already existed at the site but left no archaeological trace
That the builders imported their food from regions that were already agricultural
That the site never required a large workforce to be built
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Schmidt reverses the expected causality: it would not be agriculture that made the sanctuary possible. It would be the need to feed teams brought together to build that pushed people to intensify, then cultivate, wild cereals.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What have recent excavation campaigns at the site revealed?
choix: Traces of domesticated cereals dating from before 9600 BCE
Metal tools confirming a more advanced technology than expected
Remains of domesticated animals, absent from the oldest layers
Domestic buildings, hearths, burials, and water-collection systems
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Recent campaigns have uncovered domestic-type buildings, hearths, burials beneath floors, and water-collection systems, which qualifies the image of an isolated sanctuary visited by pilgrims.
